slides.say: A and B represent nonzero digits. Which of the following necessarily divides A B plus B A?
So a number plus its reversal, and there's no result to work with. No columns to read. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in numbers, and then the algebraic form.

[short pause] Let's start by plugging in. When there's nothing to read, plug in numbers. A B is seventy-one, so B A is seventeen. Seventy-one plus seventeen is eighty-eight. Eighty-eight doesn't divide by three or by ten, so choice numbers two and three are out.
Two are left, so one more number. Seventy-two plus twenty-seven is ninety-nine, and ninety-nine doesn't divide by four. Out. So eleven, choice number one is our answer.
at: choice number one is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Another way is the algebraic form. What's different? Instead of trying numbers, we write the number by its digits, and see why it always works. A B is ten A plus B, because A is in the tens. Forty-seven is ten times four, plus seven.
at: A B is ten A plus B

slides.say: And a three-digit number A B C is a hundred A, plus ten B, plus C. Five thirty-eight is five hundred, plus thirty, plus eight.
So A B plus B A is ten A plus B, plus ten B plus A. That's eleven A plus eleven B, eleven times, in brackets, A plus B. Always divisible by eleven. Choice number one.
at: ten A plus B, plus ten B

slides.say: And the minus works the same way. A B minus B A is nine times, in brackets, A minus B. Sixty-two minus twenty-six is thirty-six, four nines. Both patterns come back on the exam. Many strong students like this way, but two quick numbers are usually faster. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
